tagline.text: The only active volcano on mainland Cagayan, a caldera trek among sulfur steam

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,100–2,000 (climbing costs only, excluding flights and lodging)

children.text: Mount Cagua is an active volcano about 1,133 m above sea level in Gonzaga, Cagayan. Its summit caldera, with sulfur steam and boiling pools, makes it one of the most distinctive treks in northern Luzon. Advance registration with the Gonzaga tourism office and a local guide are required.
Mount Cagua (Cagua Volcano) is a stratovolcano in Gonzaga, Cagayan, in northeastern Luzon at the northern end of the Sierra Madre range. Wikipedia gives its height as
, while a mountaineering site lists its highest point at
, so figures differ slightly by source. It lies about
12 km
south of Gonzaga town and about
14 km
south of Port Irene in Santa Ana. It is on the list of active volcanoes monitored by PHIVOLCS, the Philippine volcano and earthquake agency, and has erupted twice on record, in 1860 and October 1907.
The summit area opens into a caldera about
1.5 km

across with steep walls. Inside are two fumarole fields, north and south: the north one has boiling pools of sulfurous water, while the south one has many steam vents. Six hot springs are known around the mountain, another sign of its volcanic activity. Locals reportedly also call the mountain "Bantay ti Apuy," meaning guardian of the fire.

There are two main trails. The most commonly used one starts at Barangay Magrafil and climbs to the north rim, while the trail from Sitio Bagsang in Barangay Santa Clara is longer, passing through rainforest and near Cagua Falls. The route is not technically difficult, but rain brings mud and leeches, and volcanic gas and boiling ground are real hazards. For planning, note that the municipality of Gonzaga manages entry by ordinance and its tourism office assigns guides. One guide covers up to four people, so larger groups need more guides, and the orientation you receive at registration covers safety rules and the carry-out-your-trash principle. Because the procedure is fixed from the start, even first-timers can take it on without much worry.

The biggest draw of Mount Cagua is that you can walk an active volcano on mainland Cagayan. Unlike Taal or Mayon, which Manila residents often visit, few people come here, so it is quiet, and after the climb it combines well with other Cagayan sights such as Palaui Island and Callao Cave. Just remember that Gonzaga runs a registration system, so you cannot enter the mountain if you simply show up.
This is the first ridge you reach after climbing from Magrafil. The grassy slope opens up and you can see the whole caldera and the Sierra Madre ranges at once. The north rim, at about
above sea level, is often the goal of a day hike. On clear early mornings, clouds settle below the caldera and make for good photos.
The north fumarole near the caldera floor has boiling sulfur pools, and the smell of sulfur becomes strong from about
above sea level. It is about a
20-minute
walk from the campsite, and the ground in places is only a thin crust, so walk only on the path your guide chooses.
It has more steam vents spread out than the north one and almost no pools. It lies along the forest path toward the south rim and summit, so it fits well into the second day of an overnight climb.
A campsite sits on a forested flat in the middle of the caldera, with a water source nearby. Space is limited, so ask about other groups' schedules when you register.
This forest trail follows an old logging road and hunters' paths. You walk a rough road through cornfields and rice paddies up to about
above sea level, then enter the rainforest. The path is clear, so there is little risk of getting lost.
The trail from Sitio Bagsang in Santa Clara runs about
8 km
through rainforest and past Cagua Falls before reaching the first fumarole. The starting point is only
above sea level, so the walk is longer, but the forest and stream scenery is rewarding.

Six hot springs are known around the mountain, including Maasok, Magrafil, Manaring, San Jose, Kabillangan and Paminta. If you want a place to soak before or after the climb, first check with the Gonzaga tourism office whether they are currently open to visitors.

items.title: Classic 1 night, 2 days
items.subtitle: From Magrafil, camping in the caldera

children.text: Take a van from Tuguegarao to Gonzaga town and find lodging. Complete your advance registration with the Gonzaga tourism office a few days earlier, and buy your food in Tuguegarao beforehand.
Take a tricycle or motorcycle from Gonzaga market to Barangay Magrafil, where you complete entry registration and orientation and are assigned a guide.
Set off from the trailhead. Climb the rough road between cornfields and rice paddies, and from about
above sea level enter the rainforest.
From about
above sea level you begin to smell sulfur. Climb the grassy slope to the north rim and have lunch overlooking the caldera.
Descend from the north rim to the campsite on the caldera floor, passing the north fumarole. Set up camp and stock up on water.
Finish the round trip through the south fumarole and south rim to the summit via the forest path in about
3 hours
Break camp and start down to Magrafil, reaching the trailhead around lunchtime. The rough road on the way down can feel longer than it did on the way up.
Hiking times increase greatly after rain. Allow plenty of time for the trip back to Tuguegarao on the last day.

items.title: Day hike
items.subtitle: Round trip to the north rim

children.text: Leave Gonzaga town and head to Magrafil. Confirm the schedule with your guide in advance.
You should leave the trailhead by this time at the latest. Climbing to the caldera rim usually takes
2–4 hours
Take photos and rest at the north rim, and if you feel strong, look around just part of the fumarole area.
Start down. The descent also takes about
2–3 hours
, so adjust your plan to reach the village before dark.
If you add a visit to the fumaroles, the climb stretches to about
4–5 hours
, which is tight for a day hike.
The flight from Manila to Tuguegarao (TUG) takes about
1 hour 15 minutes
and is operated by Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines. One-way fares vary greatly by season, so check booking sites.
From Tuguegarao to Gonzaga by van (UV Express) takes about
2–3 hours
and costs about ₱200.
From Gonzaga town to Magrafil by tricycle or motorcycle takes
30–45 minutes
and costs about ₱400 per vehicle. There have been reports that a recently paved access road has shortened the trip.
Overnight buses run from Manila to Tuguegarao, and the travel time differs widely by source, about
10–16 hours
At the Tuguegarao terminal, transfer to a van bound for Gonzaga, then continue to Magrafil as above.
Bus fares and schedules differ by company, so check before departure.
Walk-in registration is not accepted at the Magrafil or Santa Clara trailheads. You must register in advance with the Gonzaga tourism office.
The registration fee (a protected-area management board, PAMB, fee) is reported to be about ₱150–180 per person, and about ₱250 for foreign nationals.

Guides cost about ₱500 for a day hike and about ₱1,000 for an overnight trip, with one guide covering up to four people. Porters cost about ₱500 for a day hike and about ₱1,000 for an overnight trip, up to 12 kg.
Fees and contact numbers change from year to year. Check the latest notice from the Gonzaga tourism office.
The best time to climb is the dry months of February–March. On dry trails the difficulty is low, but in the rainy season ankle-deep mud, thorny vines, unstable slopes and leeches make it much harder.
From May to October clouds often block the views and leeches are rampant. In any month, check the PHIVOLCS alert level before you leave. If it is not Alert Level 0, climbs may be suspended.

Whether you do a day hike or an overnight trip, the rule is to start early in the morning. Even in the dry season, afternoon clouds can blur the caldera view and make the sulfur smell stronger. In April–May, when the midday sun is strong, you will drink more water, so bring more than usual.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Gonzaga town at the foot of the mountain has basic lodging, and most climbers spend the night before and after the climb here. Check facilities and rates locally.

Eateries in Gonzaga are cheap at about ₱60–100 per meal but offer limited variety, so it is better to buy trail food and snacks in Tuguegarao beforehand. Bring plenty of cash, since electronic payments rarely work and there is no mobile signal on the trail.

When you stay in Gonzaga the night before, confirm the start time with your guide and check your gear once more. If you camp, nights on the caldera floor are cool, so bring a thin windbreaker and a sleeping bag. Cook with a gas stove you carry in, and take all your trash back down.
Register with the Gonzaga tourism office first. On-the-spot applications are not accepted.
For a day hike, leave the trailhead by 6:00 AM at the latest.
There is no water above the forest, so carry 2–3 liters per person from the lower forest.
Bring anti-leech socks and waterproof hiking boots.
Arrange your return transport in advance. There is no signal on the mountain.
Near the fumaroles, walk only on the path the guide picks. A rock that looks solid can be a thin crust.
Carry out your trash, and ask about campsite availability when you register.
On a two-day trip, the north fumarole is close to the campsite, so on the first afternoon you can leave your pack and make a light visit.
Mount Cagua is an active volcano. Check the PHIVOLCS alert level before you leave, and do not climb at higher alert levels.
The boiling pools at the fumaroles have thin-crusted ground in places, and a misstep can cause severe burns.
Breathing sulfur gas for long is dangerous, so watch the wind direction, and people with weak lungs should not push themselves.
In the rainy season, mud and leeches stretch the schedule considerably. Get down before dark.
The mountain lies inside the Northern Sierra Madre natural park, so entry rules are strict and violators are stopped. Check the latest notices.
Prepare for emergencies by sharing your medicines and an emergency contact plan with your guide.
A marine reserve island, famous for the Cape Engaño Lighthouse, about
1 hour
from Gonzaga by road and boat.
A limestone cave attraction in Peñablanca, about
2 hours
south of Tuguegarao.
The central city of Cagayan, with an airport, serving as the base for starting and ending the climb.
